implementation_notes: Ruby's blocking-receive idiom replaces the monitor structure: Thread::Queue#pop(timeout:) (Ruby 3.2+) returns nil when the budget expires, so the deadline lives in the receive call itself, and Thread::ConditionVariable#wait(mutex, timeout) gives the same shape for hand-rolled notification; Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) supplies the monotonic stamp whenever a value must be reported or a sweep decides. In application stacks the escalation layer already exists - a scheduled job (Sidekiq, ActiveJob) runs the periodic check and the error reporter or notification integration carries the alert - so the watchman is a job plus a monotonic last-seen row rather than a service. Avoid Timeout.timeout around queue operations: it interrupts arbitrary code and is documented as dangerous.
code_sketch:
budget = 60.0
loop do
  msg = queue.pop(timeout: budget)          # Ruby 3.2+: nil after the budget expires
  if msg.nil?
    alert(subject, Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - last_seen)
  else
    last_seen = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
    handle(msg)                             # arrival restarts the deadline implicitly
  end
end
pitfalls: Queue#pop(timeout:) returns nil on expiry, so a legitimate nil payload is indistinguishable from silence; push explicit envelope objects instead of bare values.
Timeout.timeout is known-dangerous (it raises asynchronously inside whatever code happens to be running): never wrap a blocking queue operation in it when a native timeout argument exists.
Time.now is wall-clock and can jump with NTP; measure silence with Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC).

A monitor thread that dies from an unhandled exception silences the watchman itself; wrap the loop body and report the crash, and remember that an unhandled exception in a thread is only visible when Thread.abort_on_exception/report_on_exception is configured.
